Assessment: The March 17, 2021 FOMC statement is distinctly dovish and growth-supportive. The Committee reaffirms average-inflation targeting (AIT)—aiming for inflation “moderately above 2 percent for some time”—and commits to the effective lower bound (0–0.25 percent) plus continued large-scale asset purchases ($80B Treasuries and $40B MBS per month). This mix of forward guidance and quantitative easing is consistent with the expectations-centric literature: commitment-based policy in the New Keynesian framework (Clarida, Galí, and Gertler) and inflation-forecast/“makeup” strategies (Svensson and Woodford, 2005) can anchor expectations and reduce the real rate at the zero lower bound. The use of LSAPs and MBS purchases aligns with evidence that QE compresses term and mortgage risk premia and eases financial conditions, aiding credit transmission when policy rates are constrained; forward guidance similarly operates through expectations channels (the Fed’s documented use of QE and forward guidance). The explicit acknowledgement of virus-related downside risks tempers the tone, but the statement’s emphasis on “accommodative financial conditions” and a commitment to maintain support until maximum employment is achieved and inflation is on track to overshoot suggest a net positive stance for growth and risk assets, with inflation expectations intended to remain well anchored around 2 percent under AIT.

Overall sentiment: moderately positive given strong policy support, tempered by pandemic-related uncertainty.
